title: 【实验中】能在光盘数据面刻出指定颜色吗？ / [Experimental] Can we burn chosen colours on the data side of a disc?
body:
Thank you for the photos, and thanks to the artist for letting you show them (◍•ᴗ•◍)

The most useful clue is something you already noticed: the random data discs burn to the end on the same drive and the same cheap discs, and the image discs don't. So the discs alone can't be the whole story, the content plays a part too. Trying Verbatim next is a good idea, as long as only that one thing changes.

About the image being accurate, then a warped band, then accurate again. On a DVD-R the place where every byte lands is set by the groove the disc was pressed with. The groove wobbles and carries addresses, and the drive writes in step with that wobble. So the drive can't just put data at the wrong angle and then get back on track by itself. One way it could happen: the drive loses the wobble for a while, keeps writing on its own clock, and locks on again at the next address in the groove. That would look exactly like what you describe. It's a guess, but it fits, and a drive that has trouble following the groove would also explain why it finally gives up near the edge.

Your last screenshot is still from the old script (it guessed "closing failed" from the time). After the `git pull` it asks the drive where it stopped. For the discs that already failed, this shows it too:

```
python -m discprobe info --drive E:
```

If you send the "next writable LBA" for one or two of them, I can turn it into a radius and we'll see whether they stop at the same place on the disc or at the same place in the picture.

title: 【实验中】能在光盘数据面刻出指定颜色吗？ / [Experimental] Can we burn chosen colours on the data side of a disc?
body:
Yay, the Verbatim disc burned to the end and Lisa is finally on a disc (ﾉ◕ヮ◕)ﾉ*:･ﾟ✧ So the cheap discs were most of the trouble.

The 5 degrees are expected, and you don't need a photo calibration pattern for them. The geometry you used was measured on a cheap RITEK disc. Discs from a different factory (or even a different batch) have a slightly different track pitch and start radius, and a small pitch difference adds up to an angle that grows from the inside to the outside. That's exactly the gradual shift you see. The calibration only holds for discs from the same batch.

So the fix is the same as before, just on Verbatim:

1. Check that the discs are the same batch: `python -m discprobe info --drive E:` prints the disc ID (MID). Old discs from your father may be mixed, so compare it on the disc you calibrate and the ones you burn.
2. Fill one Verbatim disc with random data and run `geo` on it, as you did with the RITEK one.
3. Make the image again with that new `summary.json`.

If Verbatim discs are scarce, there is a way to spend no extra disc, but it's fiddly: burn only random data in the inner part, measure it, then append the picture outside in a second session (`image --random-below-mm`, then append). It needs the first session left open, and I haven't tried that with your drive and burn script, so I'd only go there if you're down to the last few discs.

A quadratic correction that is off can easily make a few degrees between the inner and outer edge, so I'd suspect it first. Measuring the calibration disc again is the best next step. Then the two runs can be fitted together:

```
python tools/geo_polyfit.py results\geo-E-<first run> results\geo-E-<second run>

It says whether the two runs agree, and whether the rungs support a quadratic at all or a constant pitch fits just as well. If they agree and the quadratic isn't needed, burn the next one without `--correction`.

title: 【实验中】能在光盘数据面刻出指定颜色吗？ / [Experimental] Can we burn chosen colours on the data side of a disc?
body:
Thank you, the logs and folders made this quick to check (๑•̀ㅂ•́)و✧

What they show:

1. All of these are DVD+R: the cheap ones are RITEK/F16, the Verbatim ones MCC/004. Your GU70N reads the RITEK disc very cleanly (run 171005: chi2/dof 0.93, rms 0.19°) and the Verbatim disc much more noisily (chi2/dof 4 to 8, rms 0.38 to 0.53°). That's where the complaints came from.
2. The four Verbatim runs on the same disc agree with each other within 0.3 to 1.3° between 25.6 and 58 mm. So the calibration noise is around a degree, not five.
3. The quadratic correction is under 1° from end to end, and the `image` command in your log (the one with `lisa_dithered_verbatim.iso`) has no `--correction` in it anyway. So the correction can't be what moved it by 5° either.

That leaves the disc itself as the most likely cause: the disc you burned may simply have a slightly different spiral from the disc you calibrated on. The track pitch only needs to differ by about one part in a million to make several degrees between the inner and outer edge, and old discs with the same MID can come from different production runs. Two DVD-R discs from one pack agreed within 0.12° for us, but that's one pack, not a rule.

If you want to check it: burn random data on the disc right next to the burned Lisa disc in the spindle, run `geo` on it, and compare with the calibration disc. If those two differ by a few degrees, it's disc to disc. And how did you see the 5°? A photo with something that should be straight would help.

Also, sorry about the `geo_polyfit` error: the command we print uses backslashes (`results\geo-...`), which Git Bash eats. Forward slashes, as in your second try, work everywhere; I'll make it print those.

The Blu-ray idea is fun (◍•ᴗ•◍) Timing on BD-R works now (the CLV solver in PR #25), but we don't have a BD burner yet to try pictures with.

title: 【实验中】能在光盘数据面刻出指定颜色吗？ / [Experimental] Can we burn chosen colours on the data side of a disc?
body:
Nice, a WH16NS40 and 50 BD-R discs, that's a proper Blu-ray lab (ﾉ´ヮ`)ﾉ*: ･ﾟ

Burning the disc one away from the calibration disc is exactly the right test. Of your four Verbatim runs, the last two (192826 and 193456) agree with each other within 0.3°, so either of those is a good one to use.

Why random data: a blank area has nothing the drive can decode (no written sync, addresses in the data or error correction), so a read there just fails, and timing needs reads that complete. It's not so much a silly firmware limit as nothing being there to read yet. It's random rather than a picture or a texture because some textures read with a different delay, and one drive didn't like long stretches of them, so random data keeps every read alike. And yes, that disc is the sacrificial one. On Blu-ray it's the same: one BD-R filled with random data and measured, then the picture goes on the next discs from that batch.

Your custom drive idea is right about the wobble: DVD+R has its addresses in the wobble (ADIP), DVD-R in land pre-pits, and BD-R modulates the wobble too. With raw access to that signal plus a rotation encoder, you could map address against angle on a blank disc and burn the same disc, no sacrificial one at all. Stock drives just don't hand that signal out, which is the only reason we go the long way through read timing.

Multithreading the ISO: good point. Every chunk of sectors is independent, so it splits across processes easily, and for a 25 GB BD-R it'll matter. I'll look at it.

title: 【实验中】能在光盘数据面刻出指定颜色吗？ / [Experimental] Can we burn chosen colours on the data side of a disc?
body:
@LTVA1 Thanks for the photos, and I'm glad the new one came out better (◍•ᴗ•◍) Your drawing over the old burn makes the inner curve easy to see.

The quadratic didn't break the earlier burn. That `image` command had no `--correction`, so both burns used the raw calibration, and the disc sitting closer to the calibration disc is the more likely reason this one is better.

Temperature is a fair thought, since polycarbonate grows about 70 ppm per degree. But the drive doesn't place sectors by millimetres. It follows the groove molded into the disc, and the groove grows with the disc. A warmer disc is a slightly larger copy of itself with the same turns and the same sectors per turn, so the angles stay put. What differs from disc to disc is the groove itself, fixed when each disc was molded, so I don't think a thermostat would help.

How the calibration works: it's neither a high degree polynomial nor straight lines between points. Each rung is the angle between a reference sector and a target sector, read from timing. Those angles go into a physical spiral model with two numbers, the start radius and the track pitch, plus one constant offset. The ladder starts a turn or two from the reference and puts each next rung as far out as the current fit can still predict safely, so about 22 rungs cover the range. `tools/geo_polyfit.py` then refits the same rungs with a pitch that may change slowly across the radius, and that's the quadratic.

With only two shape numbers, a disc whose pitch drifts a little shows up as a gentle curve, and the ends of the measured range are where a fit is held least firmly. That matches what you see at the inner and outer edges. Your runs start at LBA 70000, about 25.7 mm, so anything drawn inside that is extrapolated a little as well.

CAV doesn't lose precision at the edge. The timing measures an angle, so a degree is a degree at any radius. It's just a longer distance out there: 1° is about 1 mm of arc at 58 mm, against 0.45 mm at 26 mm, which is why the text at the edge shows it most. The method needs a constant spin speed because the angle is read as how far the disc turned between two reads. The Blu-ray solver in PR #25 works the other way round: Blu-ray drives read in CLV, so it times the spin period in zones and gets the radius from that. On a DVD the phase timing measures the angle itself, which is what the picture needs.

More points and choosing them yourself: part of that is there already. `--max-targets` sets the number of rungs (default 22), `--ranges` where they may go, and `--reps` how many reads each rung takes. Placing rungs by hand isn't there yet. The first few have to stay close to the reference so whole turns can be counted, but after that, extra rungs at radii you pick (denser in the outer 5 to 6 mm, say) would be easy to add. I'll look at it.

Something you can try now with what you have: `geo_polyfit` can fit several runs of the same disc together, with shared geometry and one offset per run, so your Verbatim runs become one calibration with more rungs. It also tells you whether the runs agree. With the two that matched best:

```
python tools/geo_polyfit.py results/geo-E-...-192826 results/geo-E-...-193456 --write-summary verbatim_joint.json --write-correction verbatim_corr.json
python -m discprobe image --geo verbatim_joint.json --correction verbatim_corr.json --picture ...
```

For DiscImageStudio style fine tuning there are two ways. `disexport` turns a geo result into a DiscImageStudio preset, and then DIS's own test burn and photo fit work on top of it. Or here: burn the grid test (`image` without `--picture`), scan it flat at 600 dpi, and `gridscan` plus `correction` measure how much the lines bend and write a correction for the next burn. That one needs a flatbed scanner; a phone photo is too distorted for it.

Two things are coming soon. Multithreading works here now: a full DVD ISO went from about 68 s to 30 s on our machine, and Blu-ray gets the same. And `geo` will measure three points again at the end of a run and tell you if the drive changed while it ran, which a clean looking fit can't show. On our GH70N it caught a run whose fit looked fine but sat 0.3° off. Noisy runs like your first Verbatim ones are what it's for. I'll tell you when both are in the repo (｀・ω・´)ゞ

body:
@LTVA1 No rush at all, two hours on a busy evening is plenty for one step of this (๑•̀ㅂ•́)و✧ And it's lovely to hear the 5 µm disc might reach your lab.

80 rungs and 100 to the last sector: that should work. The ladder only picks from about 40 evenly spaced spots plus a few near the reference, so it may stop before 80 and say `candidates_exhausted`. That's fine, it just means it ran out of new places. It will take a few times longer than 22 rungs. If reads right at the edges fail, it skips those rungs and carries on.

The scanner calibration goes like this. One correction to what you wrote: the grid should come from discprobe, not DiscImageStudio, because `gridscan` compares the scan with that exact design.

1. Make the grid with the same geometry you'll use for Lisa:

```
python -m discprobe image --geo <your summary.json> --output iso/grid.iso --light 92
```

2. Burn `iso/grid.iso` with `tools\burn_imapi.ps1` on a disc from the same pack as the Lisa disc.
3. Scan it data side down at 600 dpi, with every automatic adjustment off, saved as PNG or TIFF. Two or three scans with the disc turned a bit between them average out scanner errors.
4. Measure each scan:

```
python -m discprobe gridscan scan1.png scan2.png --dpi 600
```

It writes one `results/gridscan-...` folder per scan, each with a `phi.csv`: how far each ring of the picture is rotated.

5. Fit the correction from all of them:

```
python -m discprobe correction results/gridscan-scan1-.../phi.csv results/gridscan-scan2-.../phi.csv --geo <your summary.json> --output angle_correction.json
```

(If the grid itself was burned with a correction, add `--base` with that file, so the new one includes it.)

6. Use it for either program:

```
python -m discprobe image --geo <your summary.json> --correction angle_correction.json --picture lisa.png ...
python -m discprobe disexport --geo <your summary.json> --correction angle_correction.json --sectors <disc capacity> --install
```

The first makes the ISO here, the second a DiscImageStudio preset.

The scan tools don't look at the rungs at all. They measure what's left over after the geometry the grid was burned with, so the correction sits on top of whichever geo result you used, 22 rungs or 80. More rungs make the starting point better, and the scan then shows what the timing couldn't.

About repeatability for masks: you're right that disc to disc is the limit. The 0.12° I quoted was two DVD-R from one pack, and at the outer edge that's already about 0.12 mm of arc. Over a small board the error is much smaller, since nearby features shift together, but for a whole disc it adds up. You can calibrate each disc with a stock drive though, it just costs part of the disc. We tried it once on the GH70N: burn random data on the inner part only and leave the disc open, run `geo` on that band, then append the picture to the rest of the same disc (`image --start-lba` plus `burn_imapi.ps1 -Append`). That band's result agreed with a full disc from the same spindle within 0.124°, and the appended grid read back exactly. The picture area then only extrapolates outward from the measured band. Your wobble idea would do this without giving up any area.

Multithreading and the end-of-run checks aren't pushed yet, so a `git pull` won't have them tomorrow. I'll ping you here when they are.

body:
@LTVA1 Good luck with the 80 rungs and the scanner this evening (๑•̀ㅂ•́)و✧ Marking every disc is a great habit, it saves a lot of guessing later. And an HSK4 class taught entirely in Chinese is impressive, 加油！

Your ring idea is close to something we've thought about too. The rings themselves would work: one turn at 40 mm is about 250 mm of track, roughly three DVD ECC blocks, enough for one rung, and at 0.74 µm wide nobody would see them. The catch is the order things happen in. A burn writes the whole disc front to back in one go, so by the time the rings can be read, the picture next to them is already written with the old numbers. They can tell you afterwards how far off that disc came out, and that's useful for the next disc from the same spindle, but they can't correct the disc they're on.

To correct the same disc, the burn has to pause. We tried that once on the GH70N with a DVD-R: we burned random data on the inner half and left the disc open, ran `geo` on it, then appended the picture to the rest. That calibration agreed with a full random disc from the same spindle within 0.124°, and the appended part read back exactly. The cost is a gap between the two parts, about 47,000 sectors, which comes out about 0.57 mm wide at 50 mm and about 1.1 mm at 25 mm. So one or two pauses are fine if the picture has a plain ring there, but a pause for every rung would cost far too much.

A neater version would use the open zones a DVD-R allows (up to three places that can each be continued later): write short random bands in the inner, middle and outer zone first, measure the disc, then fill each zone with the picture. That avoids the big gaps, but we haven't written it yet, and it still leaves the picture's outer and inner edges extrapolated a little.

Blu-ray has the same ordering problem, and BD-R also allows several open areas, so the same trick could apply. The bigger issue on BD is the one from before: timing on BD gives the shape of the spiral and leaves one overall scale open, so a per-disc measurement still needs that scale from somewhere, like the dial disc in PR #25. So I'd say: possible on both, worth it on DVD-R first, and on BD only once the scale part is sorted.

On averaging: you're right for the purely random part! It shrinks like 1/√N, so 4× the reads gives about half the noise per rung. You can already ask for that: `--reps 100` reads each rung 100 times instead of the default 24 (the run gets about 4× longer). The reads come out roughly Gaussian, and we use a robust average that drops the odd outlier anyway ✧

The catch is that not everything is random. On your Verbatim disc the four runs disagreed by more than their own error bars said they should, which smells like something slow drifting during a run (the drive warming up or changing its mood (￣ω￣;)). Averaging more reads makes each run look more precise without fixing that. That's what the new check points are for: if the drive drifts, the run now says so at the end.

About wear: each read alternates between a reference sector near the middle and the target, so yes, the sled does travel back and forth, not only the fine coils. It's about the same kind of work as a game or installer loading lots of files from a disc, so I wouldn't worry for a few runs, but a 100-reps run with 80 rungs is a long workout, so maybe let the drive rest between big runs (´∀｀)♡

body:
@LTVA1 Thanks for the full write-up, the scans and the files! The burned picture getting much straighter after one correction is great to see. On your three questions:

**The ring.** Our images don't write random data anywhere unless you pass `--random-below-mm`, so it isn't in the ISO. I looked at your first grid scan and found two rings that aren't in the design:

- The dark band inside about 24 mm is the lead-in. The drive writes it on every DVD-R, before our first sector.
- After a high-pass filter, there's a paler band about 3 mm wide, at roughly 41–44.5 mm radius. It runs right past the "F" mark. The grid has nothing there, only its lines and a circle every 5 mm.

Is the second one the ring you mean? If it's somewhere else, a crop with the radius would help. Does the same band show up on your other burns (the rosettes, Lisa) at the same radius? On our own RITEK discs, burned in a different drive, read errors pile up at a similar radius, about 42.5–46 mm. That's roughly where half the disc is written, so my guess is the drive changes something partway through the burn. It's only a guess for now.

**Slow pattern generation.** On a 12-thread machine here, a full grid ISO takes about 45 s. Nothing is printed for the first 20 s or so, while the worker processes start; each one loads its own copy of the design. It uses at most 6 workers however many cores you have, so the 32 threads shouldn't matter. If yours takes much longer than that, could you tell me how long? You can also compare with a single process:

```
set DISCPROBE_WORKERS=1
```

We should print a line before the workers start, so it doesn't look stuck. And `gridscan` taking almost 64 GB at 600 dpi is far more than it should need. That's a bug on our side.

**The curved edges.** The correction is only measured where the grid has lines, and outside that range it's held at its last value. Your first grid ended at the default 56 mm, and gridscan measured it over 25–55 mm (the "trend over 25-55 mm" in its output). So the outer ~3 mm of the picture, out to 57.9 mm, had no correction at all. `radius_valid_mm` in `angle_correction.json` shows the range.

The good news is that you don't need a new disc for the next step. Your scan of the corrected grid already shows what's left, and `correction --base` adds that on top of the first correction:

```
python -m discprobe gridscan scan_after_correction.png --dpi 600 --r-max 57.9
```

```
python -m discprobe correction results/gridscan-scan_after_correction-.../phi.csv --base angle_correction.json --geo results/geo-E-20261110-220500 --output angle_correction2.json
```

Use the same `--r-max` that grid was made with (57.9 if you added it that time). Then make the picture with `--correction angle_correction2.json`. A second timing calibration probably won't straighten the edges, because the bend comes from where the correction stops, not from the timing.

- **Another timing calibration** (`geo` again) won't help the edges. The timing is fine there; the bend comes from where the correction stops.
- **Another grid correction** does help, as far out and in as the grid has lines. So the fix for the edges is a grid that reaches them, plus `correction --base`.

The second pass still refits everything from 25 mm out, which should take most of the inner curve away. The last millimetre inside 25 mm will stay a little off, so keep fine details out of it.

We see read errors piling up at the same place on RITEK discs in our GH70N (about 42.5–46 mm, where half the disc is written), and a step at about the same place on your Ritek discs in your drive points to something both drives do partway through a burn rather than to the disc. body:
@LTVA1 Thanks for the files. I don't think the second correction is the problem:

- Your scan of the grid burned with the first correction is already almost straight: across 25–55 mm the rings vary by 0.28° in total, 0.05° rms. Before the correction they varied by 2.6°.
- So the second pass changed very little. `angle_correction2.json` differs from the first file by under 0.1° anywhere.
- A correction file can only turn each radius by a few degrees. It can't add tens of turns of twist.

Tens of turns one way, then reversing around the middle of the disc, is what a geometry mismatch looks like: the disc's start radius and track pitch aren't the ones in `geo-E-20261110-220500`. A pitch that's off by a few tenths of a percent, or a start radius off by some tens of micrometres, is already tens of turns by the outer edge, and a mix of the two makes the twist change direction partway out. The same thing would explain your 8x calibration disc: with that much twist the radial lines smear into nothing, even in the part that was written before the error.

`geo-E-20261110-220500` was measured on a Verbatim disc. Which discs did you burn Lisa and the 8x pattern on? If either was a Ritek, or a Verbatim from another spindle, that's very likely the cause. A quick check is to put the calibration disc and the new disc in the drive one after the other and compare the `DVD-R MID` line of

```
python -m discprobe info --drive E:
```

If the MIDs differ, the new discs need their own `geo` run (the grid corrections then start again from that run). If they're the same, please post a scan of the Lisa disc and both `info` outputs and I'll look further.

About the 8x error: `info` on that disc also shows how far the write got before 0xC0AA0301. Your Verbatim burns that worked earlier were at 4x, right? On our side 8x was the safer speed (RITEK discs in a GH70N), but your result shows it doesn't carry over to every disc and drive, so I'd stay at 4x for Verbatim in the GU70N.

body:
@LTVA1 Two corrections to my last message, after rereading the thread:

- Your Verbatim discs are DVD+R, so `info` prints the line as `DVD+R MID`, not `DVD-R MID`. Compare whichever MID line it shows.
- The 8x screenshot already answers part of it: `Media type 9` is IMAPI's code for DVD-R, and that disc has 2,297,888 sectors. Your Verbatim calibration disc is DVD+R with 2,295,104 sectors, which is exactly the size of the ISO. So the 8x disc was a DVD-R, most likely one of the Ritek ones, burned with the Verbatim geometry. That alone explains the missing radial lines, and the write error is a separate question about 8x on that disc. So my "stay at 4x for Verbatim" was aimed at the wrong disc: it was a DVD-R that failed at 8x.

If Lisa also went onto a Ritek, it needs a `geo` run on a Ritek disc first. Both corrections were measured on Verbatim grids, so they belong to the Verbatim geometry and won't carry over.

And on the pause: your single-worker run still sat silent for about a minute, so I was wrong that the pause is the workers starting. It's the preparation before any sector is written. With workers the whole run went from 4:49 to 1:48, so they do help. We've written a change that prints a line when preparation starts, so it won't look stuck. I'll tell you when it's pushed.
